newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Europe's feeds buyers cover needs on price fall.
newsitem.headline: Europe's feeds buyers cover needs on price fall.

text.p: A fall in meals and feeds prices in Europe has sparked limited physical buying, with compounders plugging small gaps in their nearby needs, traders and analysts said on Monday.
But demand for feed was dropping in Europe and traders, already wary over currency turbulence, were reluctant to step into a market that might fall further.

"Compounders have stepped up buying mostly for the winter months -- the buyers have done a little more business ahead of their summer holidays," said analyst Arie van Dijk of market statisticians Stigevo.
In early trade on Monday, business was hampered by Chicago's closure on Friday and the continued strength of the dollar.

Traders said business in the coming week was difficult to predict as the relatively strong dollar and the prospect of potentially steadier prices -- project A was slightly easier on Monday -- was likely to keep a lid on activity.
The weather was still dominating traders' thoughts, with near perfect growing conditions in the U.S. leading some to believe Chicago-traded futures might head even lower.
Van Dijk said soybeans for November delivery might fall as low as $5.25 to $5.35 a bushel, coupled with a December corn price of between $2.10 to $2.20.
"There's a sign corn is heading to that level and there's a historical correlation with the low soybean price," he said, predicting the market's nadir in August.
Feed demand was continuing to slide in Europe due to seasonal factors and the outbreak of swine fever in the Netherlands and Belgium.
Traders said the relatively cold and wet weather in northwest Europe had also raised fears about the state of the continent's sunflower crop.
Tapioca had slipped enough to increase its share of feed mixes at the expense of grains, but analysts said a further price fall would not spark increased offtake.
Much depended on what Thailand did with its stocks of tapioca.
Van Dijk said he expected the government to apply some policy of rationing over the coming months.
"For that reason, I think a price of 17 marks for tapioca is probably the bottom of the market," he said.
Dutch compounders were believed to be holding ample stocks of the material, with cover for the coming few months estimated at between 60 and 75 percent.
